title: Data Structures: Skill Summary
intro: Mix everything from this module: list methods, sorting, tuples, sets, dictionaries, comprehensions and `collections`.

questions.prompt: `tags` has repeats. Store the different tags as a sorted list in `clean_tags`.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert clean_tags == sorted(set(tags)), 'clean_tags should be the distinct tags, sorted.'

questions.hint: A set removes repeats; `sorted` gives a list back.
questions.explanation: Set then sort: the quickest way to tidy a list.

questions.hint: The value stored under `"a"` is a list you can change.
questions.explanation: Dictionary values can be lists, and you can modify them in place.

questions.prompt: `names` and `scores` are lists in the same order. Build a dictionary `results` mapping each name to its score. (`zip(names, scores)` pairs them up.)

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert results == {names[i]: scores[i] for i in range(len(names))}, 'results should map each name to the score at the same position.'
tests.message: Pair each name with its score.

questions.hint: `zip` makes `(name, score)` pairs; `dict()` turns pairs into a dictionary.

questions.prompt: This should remove the negative numbers, but one is left behind. Fix it.
questions.solution:
nums = [3, -1, -2, 4]
nums = [n for n in nums if n >= 0]
questions.hint: Removing items while looping over the same list makes the loop skip the next item. Build a new list instead.
questions.explanation: A comprehension creates a fresh list, so nothing gets skipped.

questions.prompt: A sign-up form checks thousands of times whether a username is taken. Which structure is best for the taken names?
questions.hint: Which one is fastest at *is this in here?*
questions.explanation: Membership tests on a set stay fast however big it gets.

questions.prompt: `people` is a list of `(name, age)` tuples. Store the names sorted from youngest to oldest in `youngest_first`. (Hint: tuples sort by their first item.)
questions.solution:
pairs = sorted((age, name) for name, age in people)
youngest_first = [name for age, name in pairs]

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert youngest_first == [n for a, n in sorted((a, n) for n, a in people)], 'youngest_first should list names by increasing age.'

questions.hint: Flip each pair to `(age, name)`, sort, then take the names.
questions.explanation: Sorting tuples compares their first items first.

questions.prompt: Fill in the method so `top` is the single most common fruit and its count.
questions.template:
from collections import Counter
fruits = ["fig", "kiwi", "fig", "lime", "fig"]
top = Counter(fruits).___(1)
questions.hint: Counter has a method for the top items.

questions.prompt: `stock` maps items to quantities and `sold` lists the items sold today (one per sale). Take 1 off for each sale, and remove any item that reaches 0.

tests.name: value
tests.code:
expected = {'scarf': 4, 'gloves': 1}
assert stock == expected, 'Each sale takes 1 off; items at 0 are removed.'

questions.explanation: Changing values while looping over a *different* list is safe.
`a` and `b` are two names for the same list.

questions.prompt: `grades` maps student names to letters. Build `by_grade`, a dictionary mapping each letter to a **sorted** list of the students with it.

tests.name: value
tests.message: Group the names by grade and sort them.

questions.hint: `setdefault(letter, [])` or a `defaultdict(list)` creates each list the first time.
questions.explanation: Inverting a dictionary — values become keys — is a common reporting task.
